Stated Claim / Post Context:
Jeffrey Epstein: Trump Blames Democrats Despite His Own Ties

Jeffrey Epstein came up again as Trump told a Wall Street Journal reporter the scandal is "all Democrats," despite his own birthday letter and emails.

Actual Article Body:
Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein and Melania Trump

Donald Trump brought up Jeffrey Epstein on Saturday to blame Democrats for corruption, telling a Wall Street Journal reporter in West Palm Beach, Florida, that the Epstein scandal is “all Democrats involved.”

Video:

The reporter had asked why Trump sees corruption as a top issue heading into the midterms, after a Fox News poll found 88% of Americans are extremely or very concerned about it. Trump said Democrats are “very corrupt” and pointed to Minnesota, Los Angeles and New York. When the reporter tried to follow up, Trump asked who he wrote for. Once he heard the answer, he turned on the paper.

“You guys are worse than anybody, you know. The Wall Street Journal has lost its way,” Trump said. “But you oughta look at the real corruption. It’s Democrat corruption, and that includes Jeffrey Epstein. All Democrats involved.”

Trump’s own name runs all through the Jeffrey Epstein record.

The two were friends for years on the Palm Beach and New York social scenes. In a 2002 New York Magazine profile, Trump called Epstein a “terrific guy” and said he “likes beautiful women as much as I do, and many of them are on the younger side.” Trump has said the two had a falling out around 2004.

The Wall Street Journal is the same paper that reported on a sexually suggestive birthday letter bearing Trump’s name in a 2003 album put together for Epstein’s 50th birthday. Trump denied writing it, called the report “false, malicious, and defamatory,” and sued the Journal for $10 billion. That lawsuit is still pending. In September 2025, Democrats on the House Oversight Committee released the letter after getting the album from Epstein’s estate. It matched the Journal’s description, down to the drawn outline of a woman’s body and the closing line, “may every day be another wonderful secret.” The White House insisted the signature was not his.

Two months later, the committee’s Democrats released emails from the estate. In a 2011 email to Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein’s former girlfriend who is now in prison for helping him traffic girls, Jeffrey Epstein wrote that Trump “spent hours at my house” with a victim whose name was blacked out, and called Trump “that dog that hasn’t barked.” In a 2019 email to journalist Michael Wolff, Epstein wrote that Trump “knew about the girls as he asked ghislaine to stop.” What Epstein meant by that has never been made clear. The White House called the release a smear, and the woman described in the 2011 email previously said under oath that she did not believe Trump knew about the abuse.

Trump has never been charged with any crime connected to Epstein, and he has consistently denied knowing about the trafficking.

Pointing the finger at Democrats is not new for him. In November 2025, Trump called the scandal the “Epstein hoax” and asked the Justice Department to investigate Jeffrey Epstein’s ties to Bill Clinton, Larry Summers and Reid Hoffman, writing that Epstein “was a Democrat” and “the Democrat’s problem.

Saturday’s attack on the Journal also follows its reporting on Kimberly Guilfoyle, who resigned as Trump’s ambassador to Greece earlier this month after the paper reported she bragged that wealthy Greek businessmen were paying for her travel.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Putin is meddling in the midterms to help Trump by spreading false sex abuse claims

Moscow's operatives have revived the same sleazy disinformation ploy they used in 2024.

Actual Article Body:
Putin and Trump share a moment at a G20 summit in 2017.Evan Vucci/AP

On Tuesday, an X account attributed to a Texas man named Zyron Lewis posted a video of Lewis claiming that in 2012, when he was a middle school student, he was sexually assaulted by James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas. This allegation—which zapped across the internet—was quickly debunked. Talarico was indeed a middle school teacher at that time, and a Zyron Lewis had been a student of his. But the Zyron Lewis in the video was not the real Zyron Lewis. The real Lewis told a factchecking site he had never been abused by Talarico, and X subsequently suspended the interloper.

This attempt to smear Talarico had a familiar ring, for it was similar to an operation mounted by a Russian disinformation network in 2024 that cooked up and spread a similar allegation about Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, then the Democratic vice presidential candidate. The network fabricated a video that falsely claimed Walz had inappropriately touched a foreign exchange student when he was a high school teacher.

Disinformation trackers who analyzed the Talarico smear have attributed it to the same Russian outfit, Storm-1516, that targeted Walz. The Talarico hit is the latest indication that Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s disinformation agents are once again meddling in an American election.

As Mother Jones and other outlets have reported, for about a month, Russian operatives have been circulating fake videos on US social media platforms that hurl scurrilous allegations at Democrats. These videos—made to resemble reports from such news outlets as CNN and Mother Jones—have falsely alleged, for example, that a Democratic gubernatorial candidate recruited minors into sex work and “while working for the Girl Scouts…organized sex parties for members of the Democratic Party.”

Another video claimed that a different Democratic gubernatorial nominee had sold crack to college students, “resulting in 17 deaths.” Some of these videos said a new book that I supposedly wrote—titled Enemies of Democracy for Dummies—was the source of these disclosures, and that this book details 300 criminal and scandalous acts committed by Democratic candidates.There is no such book. My actual new book is called How Russia Won: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and the Fight for America, and it covers the decade-long twilight war Moscow has been waging against the United States, a shadow campaign that includes disinformation and influence operations mounted against every US election since 2016 to help Donald Trump. It details that smear operation Russian agents aimed at Walz in 2024, which resulted in tens of millions of Americans seeing the false charge. The false claims hurled by Putin’s disinfo crew at Democratic candidates in this election appear to have been nipped in the bud. But these disinformation operations suggest that Putin wants Trump to hold on to Congress—not surprising, given the president’s recent moves to tighten his bond with Putin and reduce, if not end, US support for Ukraine. And while the Russian effort to spread sleazy false allegations against Democrats has not yet seemed to have paid off, there’s still time left. Moreover, Putin’s operatives are most likely preparing to do what they can to exacerbate any chaos or crisis that Trump attempts to generate before, during, and after Election Day. The Talarico smear might have been smothered before it could damage his campaign, but it’s a warning sign.

The following is a slightly revised excerpt from my real book chronicling what happened during the 2024 presidential campaign, when Putin’s crew succeeded in spreading far and wide a phony sex abuse smear.

On October 5, 2024, John Mark Dougan, a former Florida cop indicted for extortion and wiretapping who fled to Russia and set up a vast network of fake news sites to spread pro-Russia propaganda—appeared on a podcast called Red Pill News hosted by Zak Paine, a fringe character who had promoted QAnon conspiracy theories and who said he had been at the US Capitol during the January 6 riot. Dougan brought to the show an anonymous special guest referred to as “Rick,” who said he was from Kazakhstan.

Speaking in English with his voice apparently altered, Rick claimed that in 2004 and 2005, he had been a foreign exchange student at the Minnesota high school where Tim Walz had taught and coached football and that Walz had inappropriately touched him. As Dougan sipped wine and nodded along, Rick told a long and involved story about his interactions with Walz that Paine characterized as classic grooming conducted by a pedophile.

There was at least one major problem with Rick’s tale—­besides its connection to Dougan. Rick said he attended this high school as part of a US State Department–­funded program, but this exchange program, as NewsGuard, a disinformation tracking news site, soon discovered, had no record of a student from Kazakhstan attending that high school at the time. The Red Pill News episode, nevertheless, was carried on Rumble and other platforms.

Two days later, the X account for The Miami Chronicle, one of the phony news sites in the Storm-1516 network, began sharing a video of Rick and his allegations, promoting it to conservative commentators with large audiences. “Did you see the exchange student from Kazakhstan who gave the interview about how he was sexually groomed by Tim Walz?” this account asked, noting that Musk “needs to hear about this.”

On October 12, Juanita Broaddrick, who decades earlier claimed Bill Clinton had raped her in 1978 and who now was a right-­wing social media influencer, put up an X post with the Red Pill News footage that drew almost a half-million views. Other far-­right accounts passed it on.

The story truly went viral after a conspiracy-monger on X who used the handle Black Insurrectionist cited the allegation. He posted a clip of the Red Pill News episode, which was subsequently viewed over 800,000 times. Then he shared supposed emails from the victim, which were quickly shown by other X users to be fakes. (Black Insurrectionist had previously spread the false allegation that Harris had been given the questions by ABC News ahead of her debate with Trump.)

Black Insurrectionist flooded the zone, putting up about two dozen X posts promoting this scurrilous Walz allegation, which were viewed over 33 million times, according to Wired. Days later, the Black Insurrectionist account disappeared from X. (Not long after that, the Associated Press reported that the account was linked to a 51-year-­old white guy named Jason Palmer in upstate New York who had a history of drug addiction and a record of alleged business fraud and who owed almost $7 million in back taxes to New York State.)

Another X conspiracist posted a video claiming he had talked to the supposed victim abused by Walz but offered no evidence to back up the claim—his video drew millions of views. A video that featured a different former student alleging that Walz had abused him popped up and was viewed over 4 million times before it was deleted. It was a deepfake. (The account that posted this video also disseminated another fake video of mail-­in ballots being destroyed in Bucks County, Pennsylvania—­a video that disinformation researchers attributed to Storm-1516—and within hours, it attracted tens of thousands of views.)

Big names joined in on the Walz smear. Jack Posobiec, the MAGA activist and onetime Pizzagate proponent who now was working for the GOP, and Candace Owens, a right-­wing influencer and conspiracist, each highlighted the Walz allegation as a matter warranting attention. When Owens discussed the phony story on her podcast, she garnered 630,000 views. Foreign newspapers picked up the story. Dougan, the former Florida cop, who had seemingly launched this information op, fanned the flames and published an article incorporating the deepfake video, the Red Pill News episode, and Black Insurrectionist’s posts on over 100 of his bogus websites.

As the disinformation campaign took on a life of its own, The Washington Post revealed that Russian documents it had obtained from a European intelligence service showed that Dougan had received funds from Russian military intelligence. He also got financing, according to these documents, from the Center for Geopolitical Expertise (CGE), an organization set up by the pro-Putin, far-right Russian nationalist Aleksandr Dugin.

The Post reported that Dougan’s contact at the CGE was its head, Valery Korovin, who’d been honored by Putin in 2023 for “services to the Fatherland” for “carrying out special tasks.” Four years earlier, Korovin had proposed to Russia’s Ministry of Defense that the CGE mount “an internet war against the U.S. on its territory.” In a letter to the ministry, Korovin had explained that cyber ops and gray-­zone warfare were how Moscow could best confront the militarily superior United States and gain equal standing with it: “The possibilities posed by internet wars really are limitless, and only with their help can we assert complete strategic parity with our geopolitical opponents.”

Dougan denied all to The Washington Post and claimed the documents it obtained were fake.

For disinformation researchers, there was little doubt this attack on Walz was a Russian active measure orchestrated by Storm-1516. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence released a statement essentially confirming this, stating that “Russian influence actors manufactured and amplified inauthentic content claiming illegal activity committed by the Democratic vice-­ presidential candidate during his earlier career.”

At a briefing for reporters about the 2024 election, intelligence officials said they were bracing for Russian operations aimed at causing chaos on Election Day and afterward, which could include active measures to undermine the vote tally and even incite violence. When Trump won the election, those operations were no longer necessary.

For more information on How Russia Won: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and the Fight for America, visit HowRussiaWon.com.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Obama, in Ohio, assails 'cruelty' and indecency from Trump and his allies in the midterm campaign

Obama targeted GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton.

Actual Article Body:
Former President Barack Obama on Saturday seized on what he described as cruelty and indecency coming from President Donald Trump and his Republican allies, stepping into one of the nation's ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in battleground Ohio.

Obama specifically targeted Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Gov. Mike DeWine, have called for its removal.

"In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to," Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has "spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she's experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness."

"There's a decency we should expect out of our public officials," Obama continued. "And I don't know what's happened where the standards of behavior are so low that somebody could run an ad like that."

Obama, 65, remains the Democratic Party's best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. He was set to campaign in Michigan later Saturday night, lending the Democratic Party his star power in midwestern battlegrounds that will help determine the balance of power in American politics next week.

Obama shared the stage with Acton and former three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is looking to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it's been a hotly contested battleground this year. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy's ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.

Ramaswamy has defended his decision to press ahead with the ad as fair game. Trump aggressively defended the ad, which has become a national flashpoint in the final days of the midterms, as he voted in West Palm Beach on Saturday.

"This is a disgrace," Trump said. "The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar and she's no good. And you know what? I don't think you can get a better reference on that." He added that if his own mother had said anything bad about him, it would be front and center.

The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton's birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her "a liar" and insinuating she has mental health issues.

Acton, Ohio's COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.

The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to appear in court and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.

Appearing before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly.

"My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it's not going to work," she said. "Decency still matters." She added: "Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won't stoop."

After wrapping up in Ohio, Obama headed to a rally in Detroit for Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official working to unite the Democratic base in Michigan after winning a divisive primary by less than a percentage point. El-Sayed is running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.

Obama's appearance in the city, which is three-quarters Black, could bolster El-Sayed's support among Black voters. In the primary, his opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.

El-Sayed criticized Obama after his 2012 reelection for not following through on all of his progressive campaign promises, writing that Obama "was not the right choice — he just wasn't the wrong one."

El-Sayed told reporters earlier this month that he appreciated the former president, calling him "foundational" to his ability to run for office, but he still disagreed with elements of Obama's presidency.

Michigan also has open races for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, is slated to appear on the ballot alongside others. Benson is running against Republican Rep. John James.

Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is slated to speak in Georgia Saturday.

In Ohio, Obama also criticized Trump for failing to lower costs, a key campaign promise, saying the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn.

"I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation," he quipped. "He should be on HGTV." He went on: "There's gold everywhere. He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."

The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Trump's allies, he said.

"We're not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people," Obama said. "After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence … you get a chance to say enough is enough."

In a 2002 New York Magazine profile, Trump called Epstein a “terrific guy” and said he “likes beautiful women as much as I do, and many of them are on the younger side.” Trump has said the two had a falling out around 2004.

The Wall Street Journal is the same paper that reported on a sexually suggestive birthday letter bearing Trump’s name in a 2003 album put together for Epstein’s 50th birthday. Trump denied writing it, called the report “false, malicious, and defamatory,” and sued the Journal for $10 billion. That lawsuit is still pending. In September 2025, Democrats on the House Oversight Committee released the letter after getting the album from Epstein’s estate. It matched the Journal’s description, down to the drawn outline of a woman’s body and the closing line, “may every day be another wonderful secret.” The White House insisted the signature was not his.

Two months later, the committee’s Democrats released emails from the estate. In a 2011 email to Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein’s former girlfriend who is now in prison for helping him traffic girls, Jeffrey Epstein wrote that Trump “spent hours at my house” with a victim whose name was blacked out, and called Trump “that dog that hasn’t barked.” In a 2019 email to journalist Michael Wolff, Epstein wrote that Trump “knew about the girls as he asked ghislaine to stop.” What Epstein meant by that has never been made clear. The White House called the release a smear, and the woman described in the 2011 email previously said under oath that she did not believe Trump knew about the abuse.

Trump has never been charged with any crime connected to Epstein, and he has consistently denied knowing about the trafficking.

Pointing the finger at Democrats is not new for him. In November 2025, Trump called the scandal the “Epstein hoax” and asked the Justice Department to investigate Jeffrey Epstein’s ties to Bill Clinton, Larry Summers and Reid Hoffman, writing that Epstein “was a Democrat” and “the Democrat’s problem.

Saturday’s attack on the Journal also follows its reporting on Kimberly Guilfoyle, who resigned as Trump’s ambassador to Greece earlier this month after the paper reported she bragged that wealthy Greek businessmen were paying for her travel.

Putin is meddling in the midterms to help Trump by spreading false sex abuse claims

Moscow's operatives have revived the same sleazy disinformation ploy they used in 2024.

Actual Article Body:
Putin and Trump share a moment at a G20 summit in 2017.Evan Vucci/AP

On Tuesday, an X account attributed to a Texas man named Zyron Lewis posted a video of Lewis claiming that in 2012, when he was a middle school student, he was sexually assaulted by James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas. This allegation—which zapped across the internet—was quickly debunked. Talarico was indeed a middle school teacher at that time, and a Zyron Lewis had been a student of his. But the Zyron Lewis in the video was not the real Zyron Lewis. The real Lewis told a factchecking site he had never been abused by Talarico, and X subsequently suspended the interloper.

This attempt to smear Talarico had a familiar ring, for it was similar to an operation mounted by a Russian disinformation network in 2024 that cooked up and spread a similar allegation about Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, then the Democratic vice presidential candidate. The network fabricated a video that falsely claimed Walz had inappropriately touched a foreign exchange student when he was a high school teacher.

Disinformation trackers who analyzed the Talarico smear have attributed it to the same Russian outfit, Storm-1516, that targeted Walz. The Talarico hit is the latest indication that Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s disinformation agents are once again meddling in an American election.

As Mother Jones and other outlets have reported, for about a month, Russian operatives have been circulating fake videos on US social media platforms that hurl scurrilous allegations at Democrats. These videos—made to resemble reports from such news outlets as CNN and Mother Jones—have falsely alleged, for example, that a Democratic gubernatorial candidate recruited minors into sex work and “while working for the Girl Scouts…organized sex parties for members of the Democratic Party.”

Another video claimed that a different Democratic gubernatorial nominee had sold crack to college students, “resulting in 17 deaths.” Some of these videos said a new book that I supposedly wrote—titled Enemies of Democracy for Dummies—was the source of these disclosures, and that this book details 300 criminal and scandalous acts committed by Democratic candidates.There is no such book. My actual new book is called How Russia Won: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and the Fight for America, and it covers the decade-long twilight war Moscow has been waging against the United States, a shadow campaign that includes disinformation and influence operations mounted against every US election since 2016 to help Donald Trump. It details that smear operation Russian agents aimed at Walz in 2024, which resulted in tens of millions of Americans seeing the false charge. The false claims hurled by Putin’s disinfo crew at Democratic candidates in this election appear to have been nipped in the bud. But these disinformation operations suggest that Putin wants Trump to hold on to Congress—not surprising, given the president’s recent moves to tighten his bond with Putin and reduce, if not end, US support for Ukraine. And while the Russian effort to spread sleazy false allegations against Democrats has not yet seemed to have paid off, there’s still time left. Moreover, Putin’s operatives are most likely preparing to do what they can to exacerbate any chaos or crisis that Trump attempts to generate before, during, and after Election Day. The Talarico smear might have been smothered before it could damage his campaign, but it’s a warning sign.

The following is a slightly revised excerpt from my real book chronicling what happened during the 2024 presidential campaign, when Putin’s crew succeeded in spreading far and wide a phony sex abuse smear.

On October 5, 2024, John Mark Dougan, a former Florida cop indicted for extortion and wiretapping who fled to Russia and set up a vast network of fake news sites to spread pro-Russia propaganda—appeared on a podcast called Red Pill News hosted by Zak Paine, a fringe character who had promoted QAnon conspiracy theories and who said he had been at the US Capitol during the January 6 riot. Dougan brought to the show an anonymous special guest referred to as “Rick,” who said he was from Kazakhstan.

Speaking in English with his voice apparently altered, Rick claimed that in 2004 and 2005, he had been a foreign exchange student at the Minnesota high school where Tim Walz had taught and coached football and that Walz had inappropriately touched him. As Dougan sipped wine and nodded along, Rick told a long and involved story about his interactions with Walz that Paine characterized as classic grooming conducted by a pedophile.

There was at least one major problem with Rick’s tale—­besides its connection to Dougan. Rick said he attended this high school as part of a US State Department–­funded program, but this exchange program, as NewsGuard, a disinformation tracking news site, soon discovered, had no record of a student from Kazakhstan attending that high school at the time. The Red Pill News episode, nevertheless, was carried on Rumble and other platforms.

Two days later, the X account for The Miami Chronicle, one of the phony news sites in the Storm-1516 network, began sharing a video of Rick and his allegations, promoting it to conservative commentators with large audiences. “Did you see the exchange student from Kazakhstan who gave the interview about how he was sexually groomed by Tim Walz?” this account asked, noting that Musk “needs to hear about this.”

On October 12, Juanita Broaddrick, who decades earlier claimed Bill Clinton had raped her in 1978 and who now was a right-­wing social media influencer, put up an X post with the Red Pill News footage that drew almost a half-million views. Other far-­right accounts passed it on.

The story truly went viral after a conspiracy-monger on X who used the handle Black Insurrectionist cited the allegation. He posted a clip of the Red Pill News episode, which was subsequently viewed over 800,000 times. Then he shared supposed emails from the victim, which were quickly shown by other X users to be fakes. (Black Insurrectionist had previously spread the false allegation that Harris had been given the questions by ABC News ahead of her debate with Trump.)

Black Insurrectionist flooded the zone, putting up about two dozen X posts promoting this scurrilous Walz allegation, which were viewed over 33 million times, according to Wired. Days later, the Black Insurrectionist account disappeared from X. (Not long after that, the Associated Press reported that the account was linked to a 51-year-­old white guy named Jason Palmer in upstate New York who had a history of drug addiction and a record of alleged business fraud and who owed almost $7 million in back taxes to New York State.)

Another X conspiracist posted a video claiming he had talked to the supposed victim abused by Walz but offered no evidence to back up the claim—his video drew millions of views. A video that featured a different former student alleging that Walz had abused him popped up and was viewed over 4 million times before it was deleted. It was a deepfake. (The account that posted this video also disseminated another fake video of mail-­in ballots being destroyed in Bucks County, Pennsylvania—­a video that disinformation researchers attributed to Storm-1516—and within hours, it attracted tens of thousands of views.)

Big names joined in on the Walz smear. Jack Posobiec, the MAGA activist and onetime Pizzagate proponent who now was working for the GOP, and Candace Owens, a right-­wing influencer and conspiracist, each highlighted the Walz allegation as a matter warranting attention. When Owens discussed the phony story on her podcast, she garnered 630,000 views. Foreign newspapers picked up the story. Dougan, the former Florida cop, who had seemingly launched this information op, fanned the flames and published an article incorporating the deepfake video, the Red Pill News episode, and Black Insurrectionist’s posts on over 100 of his bogus websites.

As the disinformation campaign took on a life of its own, The Washington Post revealed that Russian documents it had obtained from a European intelligence service showed that Dougan had received funds from Russian military intelligence. He also got financing, according to these documents, from the Center for Geopolitical Expertise (CGE), an organization set up by the pro-Putin, far-right Russian nationalist Aleksandr Dugin.

The Post reported that Dougan’s contact at the CGE was its head, Valery Korovin, who’d been honored by Putin in 2023 for “services to the Fatherland” for “carrying out special tasks.” Four years earlier, Korovin had proposed to Russia’s Ministry of Defense that the CGE mount “an internet war against the U.S. on its territory.” In a letter to the ministry, Korovin had explained that cyber ops and gray-­zone warfare were how Moscow could best confront the militarily superior United States and gain equal standing with it: “The possibilities posed by internet wars really are limitless, and only with their help can we assert complete strategic parity with our geopolitical opponents.”

Dougan denied all to The Washington Post and claimed the documents it obtained were fake.

For disinformation researchers, there was little doubt this attack on Walz was a Russian active measure orchestrated by Storm-1516. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence released a statement essentially confirming this, stating that “Russian influence actors manufactured and amplified inauthentic content claiming illegal activity committed by the Democratic vice-­ presidential candidate during his earlier career.”

At a briefing for reporters about the 2024 election, intelligence officials said they were bracing for Russian operations aimed at causing chaos on Election Day and afterward, which could include active measures to undermine the vote tally and even incite violence. When Trump won the election, those operations were no longer necessary.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Obama, in Ohio, assails 'cruelty' and indecency from Trump and his allies in the midterm campaign

Obama targeted GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton.

Actual Article Body:
Former President Barack Obama on Saturday seized on what he described as cruelty and indecency coming from President Donald Trump and his Republican allies, stepping into one of the nation's ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in battleground Ohio.

Obama specifically targeted Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Gov. Mike DeWine, have called for its removal.

"In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to," Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has "spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she's experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness."

"There's a decency we should expect out of our public officials," Obama continued. "And I don't know what's happened where the standards of behavior are so low that somebody could run an ad like that."

Obama, 65, remains the Democratic Party's best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House. He was set to campaign in Michigan later Saturday night, lending the Democratic Party his star power in midwestern battlegrounds that will help determine the balance of power in American politics next week.

Obama shared the stage with Acton and former three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is looking to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it's been a hotly contested battleground this year. Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy's ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.

Ramaswamy has defended his decision to press ahead with the ad as fair game. Trump aggressively defended the ad, which has become a national flashpoint in the final days of the midterms, as he voted in West Palm Beach on Saturday.

"This is a disgrace," Trump said. "The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar and she's no good. And you know what? I don't think you can get a better reference on that." He added that if his own mother had said anything bad about him, it would be front and center.

The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton's birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her "a liar" and insinuating she has mental health issues.

Acton, Ohio's COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.

The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to appear in court and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.

Appearing before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly.

"My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it's not going to work," she said. "Decency still matters." She added: "Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won't stoop."

After wrapping up in Ohio, Obama headed to a rally in Detroit for Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official working to unite the Democratic base in Michigan after winning a divisive primary by less than a percentage point. El-Sayed is running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.

Obama's appearance in the city, which is three-quarters Black, could bolster El-Sayed's support among Black voters. In the primary, his opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.

El-Sayed criticized Obama after his 2012 reelection for not following through on all of his progressive campaign promises, writing that Obama "was not the right choice — he just wasn't the wrong one."

El-Sayed told reporters earlier this month that he appreciated the former president, calling him "foundational" to his ability to run for office, but he still disagreed with elements of Obama's presidency.

Michigan also has open races for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, is slated to appear on the ballot alongside others. Benson is running against Republican Rep. John James.

Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is slated to speak in Georgia Saturday.

In Ohio, Obama also criticized Trump for failing to lower costs, a key campaign promise, saying the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn.

"I don't know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation," he quipped. "He should be on HGTV." He went on: "There's gold everywhere. He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."

The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Trump's allies, he said.

"We're not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people," Obama said. "After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence … you get a chance to say enough is enough."
